\chapter{When You Are Lost}
\label{ch:ur-when-you-are-lost}
\hlchaptermodality{22}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I have not understood, ask what somebody said, and ask them to say it again gently -- three sentences that need no letter this book has not taught.}

A learner who has stopped following says so, asks for the words back, and asks for them slower: maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā, kyā kahā, ārām se kaheṅ -- a repair kit this track did not have at all four chapters ago.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kahnā]{\ur{کہنا} (kahnā) — to say}

\label{lesson:UR-C22-kahna}



\begin{quote}
Chapter six taught \emph{bolnā}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} — a word whose opening letter is still ahead of you in the script ladder, so it stays in romanization here. Urdu has a second verb here, and the line between them is the line between the act and the words.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the complementiser two lessons back — \emph{ki}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کہنا}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کہنا}} — \emph{kahnā} — \textbf{to say, to tell}
\end{quote}

Four letters, all of them yours: \textbf{\ur{ک}}\ur{،} \textbf{\ur{ہ}}\ur{،} \textbf{\ur{ن}}\ur{،} \textbf{\ur{ا}}. Strip the \textbf{-\ur{نا}} of chapter six and the stem is \textbf{\ur{کہ}-}.

\emph{bolnā} is about producing speech — \emph{maiṅ urdū boltā hūṅ}, I speak Urdu. \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} is about the content — what somebody actually said. English merges the two under \emph{speak} and \emph{say} without a clean rule; Urdu keeps them apart, and after \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} the clause introduced by \textbf{\ur{کہ}} follows naturally.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{کہنا}} is Sanskrit \emph{kathayati}, \textquotedblleft{}to tell, to relate,\textquotedblright{} on the noun \emph{kathā}, \textquotedblleft{}a story.\textquotedblright{} That noun is still in Urdu as \textbf{\ur{کہانی}}, \emph{kahānī}, \textquotedblleft{}a tale\textquotedblright{} — the word a chapter-seventeen writing lesson already put in front of you. \emph{To say} and \emph{a story} are one root, two syllables apart.

Its stem \textbf{\ur{کہ}-} looks exactly like the borrowed complementiser \textbf{\ur{کہ}} of the last chapter and has nothing to do with it: one is inherited from Sanskrit, the other borrowed from Persian, and they collided on the page. Urdu is full of these seams.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kahnā}, then the stem — \emph{kah-}
  \item the pair, and hear the line between them — \emph{bolnā … kahnā}
  \item \emph{maiṅ kahtā hūṅ ki …} — I say that …
  \item the word and the story — \emph{kahnā … kahānī}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What separates \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} from \emph{bolnā}? (\emph{bolnā} is producing speech; \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} is what was said.) Which noun shares its root? (\textbf{\ur{کہانی}}, a story.) And is its stem the same word as the \textbf{\ur{کہ}} of the last chapter? (\textbf{No} — one inherited, one borrowed, and they only look alike.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kyā kahā?]{\ur{کیا} \ur{کہا؟} — what did you say?}

\label{lesson:UR-C22-kya-kaha}



\begin{quote}
Chapter nineteen gave you the first thing a lost learner says. This is the second, and it is made of the verb from the lesson before and one word from chapter three.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the sentence chapter one deferred — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{کیا} \ur{کہا؟}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{کیا} \ur{کہا؟}} — \emph{kyā kahā?} — \textbf{what did you say?}
\end{quote}

Two words. \textbf{\ur{کیا}} is the \emph{what} of chapter three, back in the middle of the sentence where it means \emph{what} rather than marking a yes-or-no question — the distinction the nineteenth chapter drew. \textbf{\ur{کہا}} is \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} in the past, the form you use for something that has already been said.

Say it with the voice rising and it is a request to repeat. Said flatly, with a frown, it is a challenge — so the tune matters more here than in any sentence this book has taught.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the repair kit, in three sentences}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{say} \\
\midrule
you did not follow at all & \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} \\
you did not catch the words & \emph{kyā kahā?} \\
you want it slower & the next lesson \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not one of these needed a new word before this chapter. \textbf{\ur{کیا}} has been in the book since chapter three, \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} since chapter one, and \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} arrived one lesson ago. What was missing was somebody putting them next to each other.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kyā kahā?} — rising, as a request
  \item the two together — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā … kyā kahā?}
  \item and close it politely — \emph{shukriyā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which chapter taught each half of \textbf{\ur{کیا} \ur{کہا؟}} (\textbf{\ur{کیا}} in chapter three; \textbf{\ur{کہنا}}, whose past this is, one lesson ago.) Is the \textbf{\ur{کیا}} here the question-marker of chapter nineteen? (\textbf{No} — it is in the middle, so it means \emph{what}.) And what changes it from a request into a challenge? (\textbf{The tune}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ārām se]{\ur{آرام} \ur{سے} — slowly, gently}

\label{lesson:UR-C22-aram-se}



\begin{quote}
Asking somebody to say it again only helps if they say it again at a speed you can follow.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the request from the lesson before — \emph{kyā kahā?}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ur{آرام} \ur{سے}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آرام} \ur{سے}} — \emph{ārām se} — \textbf{slowly; gently; take your time.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ur{آرام} \ur{سے} \ur{کہیں}} — \emph{ārām se kaheṅ} — \textbf{please say it slowly.}
\end{quote}

The wave over the first letter is the \emph{alif madda} of chapter seven. \textbf{\ur{سے}} is the postposition \emph{with}, so the phrase is literally \emph{with ease} — and the second word is the same \textbf{\ur{سے}} the book has been showing since chapter three in \emph{āp se mil kar}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ur{آرام}} is Persian \emph{ārām}, \textquotedblleft{}rest, ease, repose,\textquotedblright{} on an old Indo-Iranian root for standing still. So Urdu's way of asking somebody to slow down does not ask them to be \textbf{slow}; it asks them to be \textbf{at ease}. That is a gentler thing to say to a stranger than the English request, and it is why \emph{ārām se} also means \emph{take it easy}, \emph{carefully}, and \emph{no rush} depending on where it lands.

\textbf{\ur{کہیں}} is \textbf{\ur{کہنا}} in the polite request form. You are not asked to learn that ending here — only to hear that the verb from the last lesson is inside it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the repair kit is now whole}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{when} & \textbf{say} \\
\midrule
you did not follow & \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā} \\
you did not catch it & \emph{kyā kahā?} \\
you want it slower & \emph{ārām se kaheṅ} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three sentences, four chapters, and not one new letter. Before chapter nineteen this track had no repair language at all: a learner who lost the thread had \textbf{\ur{شکریہ}} and \textbf{\ur{نہیں}} and nothing else.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ārām se}
  \item \emph{ārām se kaheṅ}
  \item the whole kit in order — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā … kyā kahā? … ārām se kaheṅ … shukriyā}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\ur{آرام}} mean on its own? (\textbf{Rest, ease} — Persian.) So what are you literally asking for? (\textbf{Ease}, not slowness.) And which verb is inside \textbf{\ur{کہیں}}? (\textbf{\ur{کہنا}}, from two lessons ago.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kahnā · kyā kahā? · ārām se]{When you are lost}

\label{lesson:UR-R22-when-you-are-lost}



\begin{quote}
Three items landed in this chapter, and between them they rescue a conversation. Name all three, and say which chapter each of their pieces came from.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the repair kit in order — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā … kyā kahā? … ārām se kaheṅ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} a report — \emph{maiṅ kahtā hūṅ ki yih ṭhīk hai}
  \item \emph{Say it:} an argument — \emph{ṭhīk hai, lekin … kyūṅki …}
  \item \emph{Recall:} seven lessons back, the reason word and the two words inside it — \emph{kyūṅki}
  \item \emph{Recall:} twelve lessons back, the joiner that adds — \emph{aur}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — the first conversation, rescued}
The exchange this book opened with was taught between eighty and a hundred lessons ago and has not been asked for since. It is also the exact place a beginner gets lost — so run it now, cold, and put the repair kit inside it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the opening, from memory — \emph{salām … āp kā nām kyā hai?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} your answer, and the courtesy after it — \emph{merā nām … hai. āp se mil kar khushī huī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the wellbeing question respectfully, choosing for a man or a woman — \emph{āp kaise haiṅ? / āp kaisī haiṅ?}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the reply — \emph{maiṅ ṭhīk hūṅ, shukriyā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} now lose the thread, and rescue it — \emph{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā. kyā kahā? ārām se kaheṅ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} and close — \emph{khudā hāfiz}
  \item \emph{Recall:} which of \emph{āp}, \emph{tum} and \emph{tū} you used, and why
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Four chapters ago this book could not deny a sentence, ask a yes-or-no question, join two nouns, give a reason, or say that it had not understood. Say the sentence chapter one promised and never delivered. (\emph{\textbf{maiṅ nahīṅ samajhtā}}.) Say the question that asks for a repeat. (\textbf{\ur{کیا} \ur{کہا؟}}) And say the four members of the \textbf{k-} family. (\emph{\textbf{kyā, kahāṅ, kyūṅ, kaun}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
